The Achaemenid Persian Empire. Between 550 and 330 BCE, this was the ancient world's largest territorial state, stretching from the Mediterranean to the Indus River and from Central Asia to Egypt. Founded by Cyrus the Great, the Achaemenids pioneered something revolutionary—an empire based on cultural tolerance and trade rather than terror.

Cyrus unified the Persian tribes and founded the dynasty by conquering the Median empire, then the Lydian kingdom, absorbing its wealth in gold, and finally Babylon in 539 BCE. What set Cyrus apart was his approach: he allowed conquered peoples to keep their religions, languages, and local rulers, called satraps, in exchange for taxes and loyalty. This satrap system became the model for all subsequent imperial administration. He founded Pasargadae as the ceremonial capital and promoted the construction of the Royal Road, the first major infrastructure project designed to unify a continental empire.

The empire reached its territorial and cultural peak under Darius I and Xerxes I. Darius, ruling from 522 to 486 BCE, expanded the empire to its greatest extent, from the Danube River to the Indus. He divided it into twenty provinces with appointed governors, standardized taxation, and a unified legal code. He also introduced the daric, a gold coin, establishing a common currency across the empire and facilitating trade.

Xerxes I, who ruled from 486 to 465 BCE, conducted the famous invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. He was defeated at the naval battle of Salamis and at Plataea, then focused on consolidating Persian control of the Near East.

The empire adopted Zoroastrianism, the monotheistic faith centered on Ahura Mazda, the wise lord, and made it the state religion. Yet they tolerated local cults and allowed the Jews to rebuild the Temple of Jerusalem. The satrap system maintained unity—provincial governors held administrative and military power but answered to the king. The royal road allowed rapid communication and military mobilization. Persia became a nexus of trade—the Silk Road and Mediterranean commerce enriched the empire and spread Persian cultural influence to India, Egypt, and Greece.

Alexander the Great of Macedon eventually defeated the last Achaemenid king, Darius III, at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE, ending Persian rule, though Hellenistic and Parthian Persia would remain major powers for centuries to come.
